newsitem.title: USA: Ethics panel gives Justice tape of Gingrich call.
newsitem.headline: Ethics panel gives Justice tape of Gingrich call.

text.p: The House of Representatives ethics panel on Monday turned over to the Justice Department a tape of an intercepted telephone call by House Speaker Newt Gingrich after receiving it from the senior Democrat on the committee.

A Florida couple active in Democratic politics on Monday said they had delivered a tape of the controversial conference call between Gingrich and his top lieutenants, one of whom was using a cellular phone, to Representative Jim McDermott of Washington.
A transcript of the tape was published in two newspapers two days later, prompting Republican calls for an FBI criminal investigation into the source of the leak.
It is a federal crime to intentionally intercept telephone calls or disclose their content.

Confirmation that McDermott had received the tape, and the ethics committee's decision to turn it over to federal criminal investigators, turned the last stages of the ethics investigation of Gingrich into a major embarrassment for the Democrats.

"If in fact Congressman McDermott is responsible for the leak, he should resign from Congress immediately," said Representative John Boehner, chairman of the House Republican Conference, who was a participant in the conference call.

In a statement, McDermott said: "I have communicated with the chair of the Committee on Standards of Official Conduct (ethics committee). It is therefore an issue before the committee. I have not made comments about the substance before the committee in the past. I will make no comment now."

But Theodore Van Der Meid, chief counsel for the ethics committee, sent McDermott a letter late on Monday saying the panel had decided not to accept the materials from McDermott, turning them over instead to the Justice Department.

"By direction of the chair and after consultation with the chief of the criminal division of the Department of Justice, the contents of the envelope including the audio cassette tape and the cover letter were hand delivered to the Department of Justice this evening," he said. A copy of the letter was released to Reuters.
No comment was immediately available from McDermott or the Justice Department. A White House spokesman declined comment.
The New York Times, in publishing transcripts, said the tapes came from a Democrat in Congress opposed to Gingrich.

The latest twist in the Gingrich ethics saga began on Monday in Gainesville, Florida, where John and Alice Martin appeared with a lawyer, explaining how they picked up the conference call on a police scanner while riding in their car near Jacksonville.
They recognised some of the voices, used a tape recorder in the car to record the call and gave the tape to McDermott when they were in Washington.
They had been referred to McDermott last Wednesday by Representative Karen Thurman, a Florida Democrat, and sought him out at the ethics committee's room in the basement of the Capitol.
"We told him we had something to turn over to the ethics committee ... He took the envelope (containing the tape) in his hand and said he would listen to it," Mrs. Martin said.
The conversation took place on Dec. 21, the day the ethics committee said Gingrich had violated House rules and he admitted doing so.
When the transcripts were published on Friday Democrats said they showed Gingrich was violating a pledge not to orchestrate his public defence in the ethics case. Republicans deny the accusation.
The House is due to vote next Tuesday, the day after President Clinton's inauguration, on a punishment for Gingrich for his ethics violation.
